title: 17th Annual Pershing Square Value Investing and Philanthropy Challenge
description: 17th Annual Pershing Square Value Investing and Philanthropy Challenge
summary: The talk presents a mixed view on Amazon and Warner Bros. Discovery regarding their interest in acquiring UFC and other international media rights, noting Netflix's precedent with WWE. It offers a bullish case for Vail Resorts, citing its irreplaceable ski resort network, strong capital allocation history, and potential for earnings reacceleration despite recent weather challenges. Conversely, the discussion on AutoZone is bearish, highlighting concerns over softline share loss, margin compression, and operational under-investment.
thesis: The talk presents a mixed view on Amazon and Warner Bros. Discovery regarding their interest in acquiring UFC and other international media rights, noting Netflix's precedent with WWE. It offers a bullish case for Vail Resorts, citing its irreplaceable ski resort network, strong capital allocation history, and potential for earnings reacceleration despite recent weather challenges. Conversely, the discussion on AutoZone is bearish, highlighting concerns over softline share loss, margin compression, and operational under-investment.

claims.claim: Amazon has a strong interest in acquiring UFC rights as a global popular asset that fits well into their portfolio.
claims.quote: We also spoke with a strategist at Amazon who indicated to us that they have a very strong interest in a global popular asset like the UFC that fits well into their portfolio.
claims.speaker: John

claims.claim: Warner Bros. Discovery is a potential buyer of a bundled international media rights deal for UFC.
claims.quote: From speaking to several experts, Amazon, Eurosport, and ESPN are potential buyers of such a bundle deal.
claims.speaker: Jill

claims.claim: Netflix acquired WWE's international rights as part of a bundle, setting a precedent for future deals.
claims.quote: We've seen earlier this year that Netflix acquired WWE's international right as part of the bundle, and they set a precedent that has never happened in industry.
claims.speaker: Jill

claims.claim: Comcast is bidding to take Warner Bros.' NBA package from ESPN at a 2.1 times step up.
claims.quote: just this morning, there was a surprise announcement that Comcast was gonna bid a 2.1 times step up and take Warner Bros.' NBA package from that.
claims.speaker: John

claims.claim: Google is mentioned as a competitor to Amazon in the context of sports media rights.
claims.quote: ESPN and Amazon are going to fight aggressively over this asset. There's also strong interest from other players as well, like Fox Sports, Netflix, Warner Bros. Discovery, Peacock and Apple TV.
claims.speaker: John

claims.claim: Valvoline is positioned to become an industry leader similar to AutoZone and O'Reilly by growing net income while strategically repurchasing shares.
claims.quote: And Valvoline's commitment to returning cash to shareholders, its robust economics, position it to become another industry cannibal like AutoZone and O'Reilly, who've been able to substantially grow net income while strategically repurchasing shares with fuel share price appreciation.
claims.speaker: null

claims.claim: The precedent set by AutoZone and O'Reilly raises confidence that Valvoline can achieve similar results of growing net income and repurchasing shares.
claims.quote: The precedent they set raises our level of confidence that Valvoline will be able to do the same.
claims.speaker: null

claims.claim: AutoZone and O'Reilly have successfully grown net income while strategically repurchasing shares, serving as a benchmark for Valvoline.
claims.quote: who've been able to substantially grow net income while strategically repurchasing shares with fuel share price appreciation.
claims.speaker: null

claims.claim: The speaker believes ASO (AZO) is losing share in softlines vendors like Nike and will face margin compression as its product mix worsens from softlines to hardlines.
claims.quote: So we believe that ASO is losing share in the softlines vendors. So like Nike is obviously one of the largest ones. On the hardlines, so hardlines are like lower margin than softlines, So as you lose share and you sort of like, you know, make your product mix worsen from softlines to hardlines, there'll be a margin compression as well there.
claims.speaker: null

claims.claim: The speaker holds a negative view on ASO's softline business due to an inability to attract footfall, which will lead to weakness in both hardlines and softlines.
claims.quote: To summarize, you know, you're absolutely right, softlines tend to have higher margin and they also have shorter purchase cycles, which is why we see Hibbett and Dick's positioned better. You know, they obviously do softline, but our negative view on softline specifically for ASO comes from the lack of ability to attract footfall, because hardlines will be impacted and therefore, they will have weakness in softlines.
claims.speaker: null

claims.claim: The speaker expects ASO's net leverage to rise to 2.5X as EBITDA and free cash flow decline due to opening new stores in mature markets and impaired operations.
claims.quote: So both of these will lead to a much lower FCF, and although the balance sheet is not stressed right now, as our EBITDA declines and as our FCF also declines, we think that going ahead, the net leverage raises to 2.5X. That being said, we don't see the company having to like raise a lot of debt to finance the new store openings because it is making cash right now. So it's not totally impaired and we don't expect it to go to zero, but it will be like significantly stressed going ahead.
claims.speaker: null

claims.claim: The speaker believes ASO has been under-investing in its business, evidenced by poor IT systems that cannot handle pricing common across stores.
claims.quote: Now, the management has been talking about these turnaround initiatives, but we don't think that's enough that can offset these margin pressures. Going ahead, if they reduce their store opening. Now, why we think store opening will happen is that A, that's how the management is incentivized, on absolute sales figures, right? So if your SSSG is is impaired going forward, the only way to offset that is to like keep opening stores, and that's what the management is even guided to.
claims.speaker: null

claims.claim: The speaker believes Vail's pricing power and operating leverage will cause earnings growth to reaccelerate, modeling 9% organic free cash flow growth over the next five years.
claims.quote: Our thesis addresses each of these concerns. First, we think that Vail's pricing power, combined with operating leverage, will cause earnings growth to reaccelerate and we model 9% organic free cash flow growth over the next five years. Second, we think that management are wise allocators of capital and while we're excited about potential upside from future acquisitions, we think they'll largely continue returning capital as they already have. And third, we think the weather this season was uniquely bad but also that climate concerns are broadly overblown.
claims.speaker: Joey

claims.claim: The speaker identifies Vail as having an irreplaceable network of 41 regional and destination ski resorts, including all four of the most visited destination resorts in North America.
claims.quote: Vail owns and operates an irreplaceable network of 41 regional and destination ski resorts, including all four of the most visited destination resorts in North America. Vail's flagship product, driving a third of revenue, is the Epic Pass. These are only sold at the beginning of each ski season and offer unlimited skiing across all of Vail's resorts.
claims.speaker: Joey

claims.claim: The speaker believes Vail has a history of compounding returns for shareholders, delivering a 17% IRR between 2006 and 2018 while growing EBITDA at 10% annually.
claims.quote: Vail has a history of compounding returns for shareholders. Between 2006 and 2018, the stock delivered a 17% IRR and a 6.8X multiple, while growing EBITDA at 10% annually and re-rating from 10X to 20X. Most of this growth came through acquisitions. In 2006 Vail owned just five resorts, and by 2018, they had bought 14 more.
claims.speaker: Joey

claims.claim: The speaker believes Vail's business day run rates are about a 30% EBITDA margin and 65% unlevered free cash flow conversion.
claims.quote: The business day run rates about a 30% EBITDA margin and 65% unlevered free cash flow conversion. Vail has a history of compounding returns for shareholders. claims.quote: And third, we think the weather this season was uniquely bad but also that climate concerns are broadly overblown. As the market begins to realize this and buy into our first few thesis
claims.speaker: Joey

claims.claim: The speaker believes Vail's stock is flat despite growing earnings 44% and expanding its network of resorts to 41, because the multiple is Z rated.
claims.quote: Despite Vail growing earnings 44% and expanding its network of resorts to 41, the stock is flat because the multiple is Z rated. And today, you can buy Vail for 9.8 times for EBITDA, which is below where it traded for most of the post-GFC period.
claims.speaker: Joey

claims.claim: The speaker believes Vail's Community Ikon Pass was introduced in 2018, after which the stock has struggled.
claims.quote: Since the introduction of the Community Ikon Pass in 2018, the stock has struggled. Despite Vail growing earnings 44% and expanding its network of resorts to 41, the stock is flat because the multiple is Z rated. And today, you can buy Vail for 9.8 times for EBITDA, which is below where it traded for most of the post-GFC period.
claims.speaker: Joey

claims.claim: The speaker believes Vail's stock is good for an IRR of 22% including dividends with a three-year target price of $337.
claims.quote: Hi. Hi, everyone, I'm Joey. These are my teammates, Erica and Kareem, and today we'll be pitching Vail Resorts as along with a three-year target price of $337, which is good for an IRR of 22% including dividends.
claims.speaker: Joey

claims.claim: The speaker believes Vail owns and operates an irreplaceable network of 41 regional and destination ski resorts, including all four of the most visited destination resorts in North America.
claims.quote: Vail owns and operates an irreplaceable network of 41 regional and destination ski resorts, including all four of the most visited destination resorts in North America. Vail's flagship product, driving a third of revenue, is the Epic Pass.
claims.speaker: Joey

claims.claim: Vail is expected to compound free cash flow at 9% into 2028 based on 6% revenue CAGR and 4% OpEx CAGR.
claims.quote: So what does that mean for long-term organic growth? We think that Vail can compound free cash flow at 9% into 2028 based on 6% revenue CAGR and 4% OpEx CAGR.
claims.speaker: Kareem

claims.claim: Vail's valuation scenarios project a probability-weighted TSR of 71% or an IRR of 18% by the end of fiscal year 2027.
claims.quote: Our base case assumes an 11X EBITDA multiple, which is about a one turn re-rate from here. and that gets us to a probability-weighted TSR of 71% or an IAR of 18% by the end of fiscal year 2027, which is July, 2027.
claims.speaker: Erica

claims.claim: Vail has the strongest balance sheet compared to competitors like Alterra, Boyne, and Powder, allowing it to outperform in downside scenarios.
claims.quote: Well, Vail has the strongest balance sheet when compared to its other privately owned competitors, such as Alterra, which sells the Ikon pass, Boyne, and Powder. And so this means that in a downside scenario where the industry is under pressure, we believe that Vail would outperform and could even go on the offensive to buy other U.S. independently owned key resorts, or possibly even one of these competitors.
claims.speaker: Erica

claims.claim: Vail returned $1.1 billion to shareholders in dividends and buybacks in fiscal years 2022 and 2023 despite European expansion plans.
claims.quote: Even in fiscal years 2022 and 2023, where the European expansion plans really picked up, they actually returned $1.1 billion to shareholders in the form of dividends and buybacks.
claims.speaker: Erica

claims.claim: Vail's midwestern and northeastern resorts have nearly 100% of terrain covered by snow-making, enabling them to recover quickly after negative weather events.
claims.quote: Vail's midwestern and northeastern resort resorts, such as Mount Snow, have nearly 100% of terrain covered by snow-making, which enables them to get back up and running after a negative weather event in under 24 hours.
claims.speaker: Erica

claims.claim: Even in the most draconian climate scenarios, ski seasons are projected to shorten by less than 1% per year over 30 plus years.
claims.quote: But even in the most draconian scenarios, ski seasons are only projected to shorten between one and two months, which on a five- to six-month total season across 30 plus years, results in less than 1% shrinkage per year.
claims.speaker: Erica

claims.claim: Vail's pricing power and duopoly structure enable mid-single digit pricing power, and they are better positioned than Alterra.
claims.quote: We believe a combination of limited supply, value proposition for customers, and duopoly structure should enable mid-single digital pricing power. In fact, we think Vail is better positioned than Alterra given two key factors.
claims.speaker: Joey

claims.claim: Vail cut the price of the Epic Pass by 20% in 2022, driving a 75% increase in unit volumes.
claims.quote: Two, while we think that the partnership model that Alterra has basically the scale to compete, it limits its price flexibility as any changes in pricing have to be approved by partner resorts, which are paid based on a fixed fee or revenue share fee. So in 2022, Vail took advantage of this by cutting the price of the Epic Pass by 20%, driving a 75% increase in unit volumes.
claims.speaker: Joey

claims.claim: Vail added 1 million users to the pass in 2022, with 75% of visits now pre-committed, mitigating the risk of a bad weather season.
claims.quote: The strategy worked, they added 1 million users to the pass, with 75% of visits now pre-committed, which mitigates the risk of a bad weather season.
claims.speaker: Kareem

claims.claim: Vail acquired Peak Resorts in 2019, adding 17 new resorts and 60 million of EBITDA with a one-time $15 million CapEx outlay.
claims.quote: Vail acquired Peak Resorts in 2019, which added 17 new resorts to its portfolio, they had a one time $15 million CapEx outlay, and this transaction added 60 million of EBITDA.
claims.speaker: Erica

claims.claim: Vail's historic M&A transactions have averaged around 200 million transaction value at 8X EBITDA.
claims.quote: On the left hand side there, you can actually see that transactions have been small historically, averaging around 200 million transaction value at 8X EBITDA.
claims.speaker: Erica

claims.claim: Vail has averaged around a 20% return on its growth investments historically.
claims.quote: On the right hand side there, we actually calculate that Vail has averaged around a 20% return on its growth investments.
claims.speaker: Erica

claims.claim: Vail's balance sheet is at 2.4 times EBITDA, whereas Alterra is at five times, making price cuts difficult for Alterra.
claims.quote: One is the balance sheet. Vail's at 2.4 times EBITDA, whereas Alterra is at five times, which makes any price cuts difficult to stomach given their CapEx ambitions and the risk of a downgrade at six times.
claims.speaker: Joey

claims.claim: Vail's survey indicates that 65% of respondents see more value in Epic than Ikon, and there is a high willingness to pay for a consumer pass.
claims.quote: In fact, our survey indicates that 65% of respondents see more value in Epic than Ikon, and that there's a high willingness to pay for a consumer pass for customers migrate the window ticket.
claims.speaker: Kareem

claims.claim: Vail's lower income families account for 14% of all skiers today versus 25% a decade ago, which bodes well for pricing.
claims.quote: This is great as it confirms that the consumer is affluent given that lower income families account for 14% of all skiers today versus 25% a decade ago, which bodes well for pricing.
claims.speaker: Kareem

claims.claim: Vail expects 1.2% CAGR in visits by 2028, which is still below the 2023 peak.
claims.quote: As for visitations, we're expecting 1.2% CAGR in visits by 2028, which is still below the 2023 peak.
claims.speaker: Kareem

claims.claim: Vail expects a 4% CAGR in labor and benefits costs into 2028, resulting in a 9% free cashflow CAGR.
claims.quote: As for OpEx, the key line to look at is labor and benefits, as that accounts for almost 50% of their cost base. Given that they increased wages by 50%, five-zero, in 2022, we're expecting a 4% CAGR in that line into 2028 for an incremental EBITDA margin of 53% and a 9% free cashflow CAGR, X any cash deployment which Erica will assess.
claims.speaker: Kareem

claims.claim: Vail's model projects a 9% organic free cash flow CAGR without assuming they take on any debt.
claims.quote: In our model we are projecting out, as Kareem laid out, a 9% organic free cash flow CAGR, and this would allow Vail to continue to return capital to its shareholders, while leaving that excess cash, that purple, for opportunistic M&A. Again, this is all organic, so we don't assume that they take on any debt.
claims.speaker: Erica
